_comment: Perf throughput baseline. CI gate fires if measured throughput < threshold_pct * baseline. Update manually when an intentional perf change lands; do NOT auto-update (silent baseline drift defeats the gate's purpose).
_calibration_notes: Calibration history. (1) 2026-05-10 (v0.1): 250-sample x 20K-variant x 2-panel fixture (10M genotypes). Measured 31.9M g/s on `ubuntu-latest`; baseline conservatively pinned at 25M g/s (78% of measured) to leave noise margin for shared CI runners. (2) 2026-05-16 (v0.3.1): fixture bumped to 500 x 100K x 2 (100M genotypes, 10x larger) so the v0.3 hot-path vectorization wins are actually detectable (at the smaller fixture, fixed overhead dwarfed the per-row-loop savings). First measurement on the new fixture: 70.84M g/s end-to-end (1.41s merge wallclock; 854MB peak RSS). New baseline pinned at 65M g/s (92% of measured) — preserves the existing 0.80 threshold-pct convention, gating at 52M g/s = 73% of current throughput. Allows a real ~27% regression to trip the gate while ignoring sub-10% runner variance. (3) 2026-05-27 (PR #13, issue #12 preflight gate): the always-on preflight feature on `merge` adds an extra .pvar read per input plus key-set construction + per-chrom shape analysis before pass 2. On the 2 x 100K-variant fixture this is dominated by Python-level set/tuple construction in `_keys_for(chr_pos)` (~600ms added on top of the previous 1.41s merge wallclock). Measurement on CI runner: 43.8M g/s. New baseline pinned at 40M g/s (91% of measured), gating at 32M g/s = 73% of current throughput — same 27%-regression-headroom envelope. A follow-up issue should thread `merge_inputs`'s pvar cache out to `compute_preflight` (currently re-read; preflight.py's docstring flags this); doing so recovers most of the gap and would warrant another baseline bump. (4) 2026-05-27 (perf follow-up): vectorized the chr_pos key path — `_keys_for(chr_pos)` / per-chrom breakdown now pack (chrom, pos) into a sorted-unique int64 array and use np.unique / np.intersect1d instead of building a Python set of 2-tuples. Local microbench (2 x 100K fixture): key-construction 88.7ms -> 35.0ms (2.5x); the id key path was left set-based after measuring np.unique on string arrays as 5x SLOWER than a Python set comprehension. CI measurement (PR #14, linux-x86_64): 48.2M g/s (2.07s elapsed, 852MB peak RSS) — up from 43.8M, i.e. ~+10% end-to-end. NOTE the local microbench (2.5x on key construction alone) did NOT translate to a 2.5x end-to-end win: key construction is a smaller slice of total merge wallclock than entry (3)'s '~600ms, dominated by set/tuple construction' framing implied. The ~210ms actually saved (2.28s -> 2.07s) confirms the dominant residual cost is elsewhere — the redundant .pvar read preflight does on top of merge_inputs, plus the intrinsic pass-2 genotype work. Full recovery toward the v0.4.0 70.84M baseline needs the cache-threading follow-up (eliminate the redundant read), not more key-path tuning. New baseline pinned at 44M g/s (91% of 48.2M measured), gating at 35.2M = 73% of current throughput — same convention as entries (2)/(3). Caveat: because this optimization (+10%) is smaller than the gate's 20% noise headroom, a regression that reverts specifically to the 43.8M set-of-tuples path would still clear the 35.2M gate. That is an inherent limit of gating a sub-20% change, not a re-pin error — the higher baseline still catches any LARGER future regression sooner than the old 40M pin did.
